faq.q: Where does electric car electricity come from?
faq.a: It comes from the national grid, which is fed by power stations, wind farms, solar parks and other sources. The cleaner the grid, the lower the car's carbon footprint.
asks: Is charging an electric car green?

faq.q: How long does it take to charge an electric car at home?
faq.a: A typical 7 kilowatt home charger adds roughly 40 to 50 kilometres of range an hour, so most cars fill up overnight. A normal three-pin socket is much slower.
asks: Can you charge an electric car from a normal plug?

faq.q: Why are rapid chargers so fast?
faq.a: Rapid chargers contain large, powerful converters that turn grid AC into DC and feed it straight into the battery, bypassing the small on-board charger. They supply 50 to 350 kilowatts.

faq.q: Why do electric cars need an on-board charger?
faq.a: Home sockets and wall chargers supply AC, but batteries store DC. The on-board charger converts one to the other and manages the charging safely.
asks: What does the on-board charger do?

faq.q: Is charging bad for the battery?
faq.a: Batteries last longest when not kept completely full or nearly empty for long, and very frequent rapid charging adds a little wear. Many car makers suggest charging to about 80 percent day to day.
asks: How should I look after an electric car battery?

facts: Car batteries store direct current, so AC from the mains must be converted to DC.
A typical home wall charger in the UK supplies about 7 kilowatts.
The fastest public chargers can supply around 350 kilowatts.
